TA-led tutorials. Each entry says what you do in it, which lecture or assignment it supports, and where to find its
materials.

## Block 2 {#block-2}

### B2T1: Cluster/EMR {#emr-cluster}

- **What you do:** You launch an EMR cluster from the AWS console in your sandbox account, step by step, and check
  that it starts. You then terminate the cluster so that it stops billing.
- **Supports:** L5 (Spark on a cluster) and A2, which runs its Spark job on EMR at two and then four core nodes.
- **Materials:** step-by-step guide on Canvas.

### B2T2: Spark/Glue {#glue-tutorial}

Two parts, each a Glue notebook in the [B2T2 repository](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l7-spark-glue).
Set up your account once with the repository's
[step 1](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l7-spark-glue#1-set-up-your-account-once) before part A.

A Glue session bills until it stops, even after you close the browser tab. End each notebook with its last cell,
`%stop_session`.

#### Part A: how Spark reads files {#glue-part-a}

- **What you do:** You run the notebook in your sandbox account and see, for each query, which folders, files and row
  groups Spark reads and how many tasks it starts. Exercises 2 to 6 then ask you to predict those numbers for new
  queries on the 36 months of taxi trips.
- **Supports:** L7 (Spark as a managed service, and its demos on reading files).
- **Materials:** the notebook [`l7a_data-read.ipynb`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l7-spark-glue/blob/main/l7a_data-read.ipynb).

#### Part B: slow queries and their fixes {#glue-part-b}

- **What you do:** You run three slow queries from L6 on Glue: input that can't be split finely enough, a join on a
  hot key and a window query. Before each run you write down how many tasks you expect, then you read the stage
  table to find what makes the query slow and which change fixes it. Exercises B1 to B5 follow, with their answers
  in commented-out cells.
- **Supports:** [L6](w2-l6.qmd) (why a cluster job is slow) and L7.
- **Materials:** the notebook [`l7b_slow-queries.ipynb`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l7-spark-glue/blob/main/l7b_slow-queries.ipynb).

## Block 3 {#block-3}

### B3T1: Lakehouse/Athena+Glue {#b3-t1}

- **What you do:** You query the course's rides table in Athena, predicting how much each query reads before you
  run it. You then copy one month into your own account and change it: delete rows, read the table as it was before
  the delete, load a day twice and repair it, add a column, and join your copy with a course table.
- **Supports:** L10 (lakehouses: Iceberg tables, snapshots and time travel) and L11, and the use and change tasks
  in A3.
- **Before the tutorial:** run the one-time setup in the repository's
  [step 1](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t1-athena-rides#1-set-up-your-account-once) (in
  CloudShell).
- **Materials:** the [B3T1 repository](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t1-athena-rides): the steps, one
  SQL file per step with the expected results, and the setup script.

### B3T2: Lakehouse/Glue build and maintain {#b3-t2}

- **What you do:** You start a ready Glue job that loads one month of rides into an Iceberg table in your own
  account, and read its script while it runs. You predict how much a query will read from the table's column sizes,
  then delete some rows, compact the table with `OPTIMIZE`, remove old snapshots and their files with `VACUUM`, and
  price the job's run.
- **Supports:** L10 and L11 (Iceberg maintenance: compaction, snapshots and `VACUUM`), and the build and maintain
  tasks in A3.
- **Before the tutorial:** B3T1's one-time setup, and the
  [B2T2 setup](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l7-spark-glue#1-set-up-your-account-once), which creates your
  bucket and Glue role. Then run the repository's
  [step 2](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#2-set-up-the-job-once) in CloudShell.
- **Materials:** the [B3T2 repository](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides): the steps, one SQL
  file per step with what to predict, the Glue job and the setup script.

## Block 5 {#block-5}

### B5T1: Course MCP and prompt evaluation {#b5-t1}

- **What you do:** You connect a coding assistant to the course MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and use the
  course knowledge base to check facts in your project proposal. Then you call the course LLM gateway with the same
  token and use Inspect, an evaluation tool, to score a prompt on held-out cases (questions kept apart from the ones
  used to write the prompt). You read and name the failures. Then GEPA, a prompt optimizer, rewrites the prompt.
  Last, you evaluate the new prompt and work out what the session cost in Canadian dollars (CAD).
- **Supports:** L15 to L17 (calling a model, evaluating its answers, the course LLM gateway) and your project
  proposal.
- **Before the tutorial:** do these at home, so the tutorial time goes to the exercises.
  1. Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), a Python package manager.
  2. In a terminal on your laptop, clone the tutorial repository with the command in its
     [before the tutorial](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b5-t1-mcp-evals#before-the-tutorial) steps, and clone
     your team repository. Check that your team repository contains `docs/proposal.md`.
  3. Install one coding assistant: Claude Code ([setup](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup)), the Kiro IDE or
     the Kiro CLI ([Kiro installation](https://kiro.dev/docs/getting-started/installation/), IDE tab or CLI tab).
  4. Sign in. For Claude Code, run `claude` in a terminal. For the Kiro IDE, open Kiro. For the Kiro CLI, run
     `kiro-cli login` in a terminal; the Kiro CLI does nothing until you sign in. Kiro accepts Google, GitHub or AWS
     Builder ID ([Kiro authentication](https://kiro.dev/docs/getting-started/authentication/)).
  5. On GitHub, open the issue "Your course MCP tokens" in your team repository and copy the token next to your
     name. Set it as the environment variable `KB_MCP_TOKEN`, as
     [part A, section 2](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b5-t1-mcp-evals/blob/main/mcp/README.md#2-set-up-once)
     shows.
- **Materials:** Use the [B5T1 repository](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b5-t1-mcp-evals) (short link
  `ilm.wiki/436c/b5t1`). Part A is in `mcp/`, and part B is in `evals-gepa/`.
- **Check your assistant's connection:** after part A's own check, ask your assistant these two things.
  1. “List what the course MCP server offers: its tools and the kinds of material it has.” A working reply names
     `cpsc436c_search` (searches the course material), `cpsc436c_read` (reads one page in full) and
     `cpsc436c_list` (lists the kinds of material, or the pages of one kind), and the kinds: guide, values,
     dataset, lens and reference. It may also name `query_kb`, `get_kb_doc` and `list_kb_topics`: the same tools
     under their old names, which keep working until the end of term.
  2. “Use the course MCP server: read the practice lens and run its lens pass on `docs/proposal.md`.” A working
     reply is a table with the lens's two questions (how often each job story happens and how fast its answer is
     needed; where each number in the data answers comes from), each classified as stated, partial or absent with
     a quoted line, and then two or three suggestions.

  The wording of the replies changes from run to run. Your model applies the lens; the course MCP server only
  provides it.
- **Where your assistant shows the connection:** in Claude Code, type `/mcp` in the chat. In the Kiro IDE, open the
  Kiro panel from the activity bar on the left and find its MCP Servers section. The Kiro CLI has no panel: type
  `/mcp` in a `kiro-cli chat` session. Each lists `436c` and `aws-knowledge` with their connection status.
- **Ask the course server:** keep using the assistant you connected in part A. These questions do not ask it to
  read your team's files. Ask each separately and check for a course server tool call in each reply.
  1. "What is our AWS budget for the term, and how much can we spend on model calls now? Check with the course
     server." A good reply says 30 USD per group lease for the term and about 5 USD of model calls per team for
     now, more on request for production use, and names the course page for each.
  2. "Which models can our app call through the course LLM gateway, and what is the most output tokens one request
     may ask for? Check with the course server." A good reply names `qwen3.8-27b` and `qwen3.6-35b-a3b` for chat
     and `qwen3-embedding-0.6b` for embeddings, and 16,384 output tokens for one request. It may add the request
     limit: 120 requests a minute per key.
  3. "We're thinking of adding retrieval (RAG) to our app. What should we check or read before we decide? Check
     with the course server." A good reply names the course readings on retrieval, the course code you can reuse
     and the course LLM gateway's limits, each with its course page.
  4. "What can the course server do for us? List what's available now and what comes later. Check with the course
     server." A good reply lists the server's tools, the current milestone, and the course checks open now and
     those that open later.

  If a reply has no tool call, ask again: "Check with the course server and show me the tool result you used."

### B5T2: behave and simulated data {#b5-t2}

- **What you do:** You write the step code for one rule of the Checkpoint 1 example with behave, and run it until it
  passes. Then your coding assistant writes a generator for a simulated data set of your own project (your SIM01),
  from a small sample of your data and the course's simulation standards, and a checker tells you whether the set
  follows them. Last, you run a scenario against a simulated data set, with its expected values taken from the truth
  files before the run, and find a planted bug from its failing output.
- **Supports:** Checkpoint 1 (your features and data set bullets) and Checkpoint 2 (step code that runs against your
  simulated data sets).
- **Before the tutorial:** do these at home, so the tutorial time goes to the exercises.
  1. Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), a Python package manager, and git.
  2. Clone the tutorial repository and install its packages with the commands in its
     [before the tutorial](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b5-t2-behave-sim#before-the-tutorial) steps.
  3. For part B: a coding assistant (Claude Code or Kiro, as in B5T1), and your team repository cloned next to the
     tutorial repository, with a small sample of your data in it: your data set's preview file from the
     [project datasets](project-datasets.qmd) page, or about 20 rows of your own data.
- **Materials:** Use the [B5T2 repository](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b5-t2-behave-sim) (short link
  `ilm.wiki/436c/b5t2`). The simulation standards are in its `docs/simulation-standards.md`: they are guidance, not
  required. Part D, sending a data set to AWS, is for after the tutorial and needs your team's lease.
